pages.x: In 1948 the National Party won an election in which only white people could vote, and began building apartheid, Afrikaans for apartness. Every South African was classed by race: white, coloured, Indian or Black. Marriage between races was banned, and towns were carved up so that each race lived apart, with the best land kept for whites.

Hendrik Verwoerd, the system's chief architect and prime minister from 1958, planned to strip Black South Africans of their citizenship, making them citizens of homelands, scattered patches of poor land. More than three million people were forced from their homes. Black schools, he said, should not teach children to hope for more than certain kinds of labour.

On 21 March 1960 a crowd gathered outside the police station at Sharpeville to protest against the pass laws, which forced Black people to carry papers at all times. The police opened fire, and many were shot in the back as they ran. The government banned the African National Congress, and its leaders went underground.
pages.of: protesters shot dead by the police

pages.x: Nelson Mandela, who had helped set up the ANC's armed wing, was sentenced to life in prison in 1964 and spent 18 years on Robben Island, breaking rocks in a quarry. Cut off from the world, he became its most famous prisoner, though his picture could not even be printed in South African newspapers.

On 16 June 1976 thousands of schoolchildren in Soweto marched against being taught in Afrikaans, the language of their rulers. The police opened fire. A photograph of a dying 12-year-old boy, Hector Pieterson, carried by an older student while his sister ran beside them, went around the world. Hundreds were killed in the risings that followed.

In the 1980s the townships rose in revolt, and the government ruled by emergency laws, jailing thousands without trial. Around the world people refused to buy South African goods, banks pulled out their money, and its teams were banned from the Olympics and most world sport. Songs and concerts demanded Mandela's freedom.

In 1989 F. W. de Klerk became president and decided that apartheid had to end. On 2 February 1990 he lifted the ban on the ANC, and nine days later Mandela walked out of prison, after 27 years. The two men then negotiated a new constitution, through years of violence that killed thousands, and in 1993 they shared the Nobel Peace Prize.

On 27 April 1994 South Africans of every race voted together for the first time. Queues stretched for kilometres, and some people waited all day to cast the first vote of their lives. The ANC won, and on 10 May Mandela was sworn in as president. 27 April is now Freedom Day.

Apartheid ended without the civil war many had feared. A Truth and Reconciliation Commission, led by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, let victims tell their stories and offered amnesty to those who confessed their crimes. But apartheid's mark remains: South Africa is still one of the most unequal countries on earth.
pts: Mandela was freed in 1990, after 27 years
All races voted together in April 1994
